Fingers usually go numb before toes on a Kenyan summit night, so hiking gloves in Nairobi belong on your shopping list before any hike above about 3,000 m. For most cold trails, one waterproof insulated pair is enough. For Point Lenana or Kilimanjaro, wear a fleece-lined mitten over it and keep a spare pair dry.

The city gives no warning. You leave a mild Nairobi evening in a T-shirt and, ten hours later, fumble with a frozen zip at 4,000 m. Below we cover which hikes need gloves, gloves versus mittens, how to layer them, what to check when buying, sizing, care and where to find hiking gloves in Nairobi at a fair price.

Quick Facts

  • When you need them: any hike above about 3,000 m, any wet Aberdares day and every summit night on Mt Kenya (4,985 m at Point Lenana) or Kilimanjaro (5,895 m).
  • Warmest option: mittens, because your fingers share warmth inside one compartment instead of four.
  • Best first pair: among hiking gloves in Nairobi, a waterproof, insulated glove that still lets you grip a trekking pole and work a zip.
  • Layering: a thin liner or insulated glove underneath, a mitten over the top for the coldest hours, and a dry spare in your pack.
  • Wet hands lose heat fast: when choosing hiking gloves in Nairobi, waterproofing matters as much as insulation in Kenya's long rains (March-May) and short rains (October-December).
  • Our hiking gloves in Nairobi: Thinsulate waterproof gloves at KSh 850 and fleece-lined mittens at KSh 499 (as listed on our product pages at the time of writing).

Do You Really Need Gloves for Hiking in Kenya?

Not for every hike. Low, sunny day hikes such as Karura Forest or Ngong Hills rarely need them. Above about 3,000 m, in rain or wind, or on any pre-dawn start, gloves stop being optional, because cold, wet hands quickly lose grip and feeling.

Kenya sits on the equator, but altitude changes everything. On Mt Kenya, frost can form at night from around 3,000 m, where days often sit between about 5°C and 15°C, and nights near the summits fall well below freezing. Add ridge wind or Aberdares drizzle, and bare hands soon stop working.

On a mountain your hands open the pack, hold the pole, pull up the hood and feed you. Numb fingers make every job slow, and that is when people stop eating or skip a layer. Good hiking gloves in Nairobi cost less than a taxi to the trailhead, so there is little reason to go without.

Gloves or Mittens: Which Keep Your Hands Warmer?

Mittens are warmer. Your four fingers sit together and share heat, and there is less surface area for warmth to escape. Gloves give better dexterity, so most hikers wear gloves while moving and pull mittens on for the coldest, slowest hours.

Think of four people standing apart on a cold night, then the same four huddled together. The huddle stays warmer, which is why mittens come out for summit day on high peaks.

Why mittens beat gloves on summit night

Summit night on Mt Kenya usually means leaving a high camp in the small hours to reach Point Lenana around sunrise; on Kilimanjaro, most routes start around midnight. The slow, stop-start pace in freezing air is exactly when hands get coldest.

Mittens also fit over a glove. Wearing a thin or insulated glove under a mitten means you can slip the mitten off for a minute to open a zip or unwrap a snack, then put it straight back on, without ever exposing bare skin to the wind.

When hiking gloves are the better choice

Gloves win whenever you need your fingers. On a wet Aberdares day you will be adjusting pack straps, gripping trekking poles, opening water bottles and maybe steadying yourself on rock. A waterproof insulated glove keeps you warm enough for those conditions while leaving each finger free. For day hikes up to about 4,000 m, a good pair of hiking gloves in Nairobi is usually all you need.

How Do You Layer Hiking Gloves for Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro?

Layer your hands the way you layer your body: a thin or insulated glove next to the skin, a warm mitten over it for the coldest hours, and a dry spare pair in your pack. Each layer can come off or go on as the temperature and your pace change.

Here is a practical system for a multi-day climb, built from hiking gloves in Nairobi that cost little:

  1. Base: a thin liner glove or your waterproof insulated pair. Wear this from the moorland upwards and on cold camp evenings.
  2. Warmth on top: a fleece-lined mitten pulled over the glove when you stop moving, at camp after sunset and on the summit push.
  3. Spare: a second pair of gloves sealed in a plastic or dry bag at the bottom of your pack, so a soaked pair never leaves you with nothing.
  4. Night-time drying: damp gloves go inside your jacket or sleeping bag overnight, where body heat dries them instead of the cold freezing them.
  5. Summit morning: put both layers on before you leave the hut or tent, not after your hands are already cold.

This is the same thinking we use in our list of what to pack for Mt Kenya, and the Kilimanjaro gear checklist follows the same pattern with one extra warm layer for the greater altitude.

What does Thinsulate insulation actually do?

Thinsulate is a synthetic insulation developed by 3M, made from very fine fibres. Because the fibres are so thin, they trap a lot of still air in a small thickness, so a Thinsulate glove can stay warm without being as bulky as a thick wool or ski glove.

Less bulk means better grip on a pole or a zip pull. Synthetic insulation also copes with damp better than down. In Kenya, where cold usually arrives with rain or mist rather than dry snow, a synthetic-insulated waterproof pair is the sensible first choice among hiking gloves in Nairobi.

What else keeps your hands warm?

Even the warmest hiking gloves in Nairobi cannot help if your core is cold, because your body cuts blood flow to the fingers first. A fleece-lined balaclava and a winter trapper hat protect the head and neck, where you lose a lot of heat. A thermal base layer matters too; our guide to thermal wear in Nairobi covers that layer, and a mid-weight fleece sits between it and your shell.

What should you check before buying hiking gloves?

Check the fit, the waterproofing, the insulation and the cuff before the brand or colour. The table below lists what to look for in any pair of hiking gloves in Nairobi, new or pre-owned.

What to checkWhat good looks likeWhy it matters on Kenyan trails
FitSnug at the knuckles, a little space at the fingertipsTight gloves cut circulation; loose ones are clumsy on poles and zips
WaterproofingA waterproof outer or inner layer, taped or well-sealed seamsAberdares mist and short-rains drizzle soak ordinary knitted gloves in minutes
InsulationSynthetic fill such as Thinsulate, or fleece liningSynthetics keep more warmth when damp than down or cotton

How should hiking gloves fit?

When you try hiking gloves in Nairobi, they should feel snug across the palm and knuckles with about half a centimetre of space beyond each fingertip. Make a fist: if the fabric pulls tight across the back of your hand, go up a size.

To find your size, wrap a tape measure around the widest part of your palm, just below the knuckles and not including the thumb. Compare it with the size chart, or send it to us on WhatsApp if you are ordering hiking gloves in Nairobi online. If you plan to wear a liner underneath, try them on together. For mittens, size up a little so they slide over your gloves without squeezing them, because compressed insulation is cold insulation.

One more test: put the gloves on and try to open a zip, undo a buckle and grip a pole. If you cannot do all three without pulling the gloves off, they will spend most of the hike in your pocket, which defeats the point.

Pro Tips

  • Put gloves on early: wear them before your hands feel cold; it is far harder to rewarm cold fingers than to keep warm ones warm.
  • Keep a spare dry: whichever hiking gloves in Nairobi you buy, seal a second pair in a plastic bag at the bottom of your pack for the descent or the next day.
  • Use a cord or clip: tie mittens to your jacket or pack so wind cannot take one when you pull it off for a photo.
  • Dry them overnight on you: damp gloves go inside your jacket or sleeping bag, never next to a stove or campfire.
  • Eat and drink: your body needs fuel to send warm blood to your fingers, so snack regularly on cold climbs.
  • Loosen tight straps: tight wrist cords, watch straps and pack straps across the chest can all reduce blood flow to the hands.

How Do You Keep Your Hands Warm and Safe on a Cold Mountain?

Keep your core warm, put gloves on before your hands get cold, stay fed and hydrated, and keep moving your fingers. If your hands go numb and do not recover, stop, get sheltered, and warm them gently against your body.

Cold hands usually mean the rest of you needs attention. The fix is often a warmer layer on your chest, a hat, a snack or brisk walking, not just thicker gloves.

What are the warning signs of frostbite?

Early frostbite shows up as skin that feels cold and firm, numbness, a stinging or burning feeling, aching, and skin that turns red or pale. On darker skin, the colour change can be harder to see, so pay attention to feel as well as look.

The NHS guidance on frostbite advises getting to shelter, removing tight items such as rings and gloves from the affected area, tucking cold hands under your armpits and rewarming gently. Do not rub or massage the skin and do not warm it against a fire or stove. Hard, frozen skin, blisters or a lasting loss of feeling need urgent medical help, which on Mt Kenya means alerting your guide straight away and heading down.

Frostbite is a real risk on windy high summit nights. The Kenya Wildlife Service page for Mt Kenya National Park is the place to start when planning a climb there, and our Mt Kenya hiking guide covers routes and seasons.

Common mistakes with hiking gloves

The most common mistake is packing knitted town gloves instead of buying proper hiking gloves in Nairobi before the trip. Knitted gloves soak up rain and mist like a sponge, then pull heat from your hands.

Other common mistakes: buying hiking gloves in Nairobi a size too small, which cuts circulation; leaving gloves buried in the pack until hands are numb; drying them on a hot stove; forgetting a spare pair; and choosing a short cuff that leaves a cold, wet strip of wrist.

How do you wash and dry hiking gloves?

Hand-wash hiking gloves in lukewarm water with a mild soap, rinse well and air-dry them away from direct heat. Avoid fabric softener, which can coat waterproof layers and flatten insulation.

Follow the care label first. Squeeze rather than wring, hang fingers-down in the shade, and keep them away from campfires. Once dry, check fingertips and seams, because small holes grow quickly on rock.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need gloves to climb Mt Kenya?

Yes, gloves are needed for Mt Kenya. Night temperatures near the summits fall well below freezing, and the push to Point Lenana (4,985 m) usually starts in the dark. Buy waterproof insulated hiking gloves in Nairobi before you travel for the trekking days, then add mittens to pull over them for summit morning, plus a spare pair kept dry in a plastic bag in case the first pair gets wet.

Can I just use normal winter gloves from town?

Normal knitted or fashion gloves from town are fine for a cool Nairobi morning but poor on a mountain. Most are not waterproof, so Aberdares mist and short-rains drizzle soak them quickly, and wet wool or cotton pulls heat away from your fingers. The hiking gloves in Nairobi outdoor shops sell add a waterproof layer, synthetic insulation, a grippy palm and a longer cuff that seals against your sleeve.

Are mittens better than gloves for Kilimanjaro?

Mittens are better than gloves for Kilimanjaro's summit night, because fingers kept together stay warmer during the slow, freezing climb to Uhuru Peak (5,895 m). Gloves are still useful on the lower days for dexterity. The best approach is to pack both: buy hiking gloves in Nairobi for the lower days, wear a warm mitten over them for summit night, and keep a spare pair packed away.

Will waterproof gloves stay dry all day in heavy rain?

Waterproof gloves keep out a lot of rain but rarely stay perfectly dry inside over a full day of heavy downpour. Water can enter at the cuff, and sweat builds up inside. Tuck cuffs under your rain jacket sleeves, take gloves off on hot climbs, and carry a dry spare pair so you always have something warm for the descent or the evening.

Final Thoughts

Zips, buckles, poles, snacks and cameras all depend on fingers that still work. For most Kenyan hikers, the right hiking gloves in Nairobi are one waterproof insulated pair for walking, with fleece-lined mittens added for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro summit nights and a spare pair sealed in a bag.
